A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CounselBench study. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports 2,000 clinician evaluations, original LLM-judge experiments, and evaluations of 2,880 adversarial responses (Sections 3–4 and appendices).

after.justification: v2 retains the clinician results and reports expanded model evaluations, few-shot experiments, annotator analyses, and domain-specific-model results (Sections 4–5; Appendices C, D, and H).

M1.justification: The two-part benchmark construction, six-dimensional rubric, single-turn response generation, sentence matching, and six targeted failure modes remain substantively unchanged. Few-shot prompting is added as an experimental mitigation probe, without changing the proposed benchmark construction or introducing a new model.

E1.justification: Both versions use 100 CounselChat questions across the same 20 topics and 120 adversarial questions targeting the same six failures. Additional models, few-shot prompting, and response-validity screening operate on these retained tasks and datasets. The mental-health QA reframing does not establish new task or population coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-5 to both judge comparisons and adversarial evaluation (Tables 3, 10, and 14). Appendix H additionally evaluates Meditron-70B, MentalLLaMA-Chat-13B, and MentalLLaMA-33B-Lora for response validity, with the two MentalLLaMA variants also evaluated on CounselBench-Adv. This extends comparison beyond the original general-purpose models to domain-specific alternatives.

E3.justification: v2 adds three-example few-shot evaluation, a GPT-4.1 response-validity screening protocol, and analyses restricting comparisons to items shared across annotator time or experience groups. It also specifies temperature 1 for the newly added GPT-5 judge. These extend evaluation design while retaining the original primary protocol; Appendix C's reported 460 shared QA pairs has unclear accounting relative to 100 questions with four answers each.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether high-quality examples mitigate adversarial failures (Table 3), whether annotation time and counseling experience relate to ratings and rationale length (Tables 6–8), and why domain-specific models produce unsuitable replies (Appendix H). These substantially extend the retained thematic error analysis and sentence-level safety analysis.

E5.justification: v2 supplements existing Wilcoxon tests and inter-rater reliability reporting with IQRs, subgroup means and standard deviations, and Kruskal–Wallis and chi-squared tests. Table 9 expands pairwise significance reporting, but the Factual Consistency significance indicators formerly in Table 1 are absent. Three adversarial generations per prompt remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: Table 1's expert ratings and the original eight models' zero-shot adversarial rates are retained. v2 adds substantial results for GPT-5, few-shot prompting, annotator variation, abstentions, and specialized models; examples include GPT-5 medication/therapy failure rates of 0.97/0.93 and 80 invalid Meditron replies among 100. One retained result also changes: LLaMA-3.3 judging GPT-4 Medical Advice changes from 0.0 to 0.01 (v1 Table 8; v2 Table 14).

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory, propositions, or proofs. The rubric and benchmark-count arithmetic remain equivalent; the added statistical analyses do not introduce mathematical derivations or theoretical properties.

C1.justification: v1 prominently claims superiority over online human therapists and describes CounselBench as the largest expert-annotated benchmark in its domain. v2 instead foregrounds open-ended mental-health QA, high ratings alongside recurring failures, and an 'among the largest' contribution. This substantively narrows the headline performance and novelty claims while retaining the two benchmark components.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the retained 72.9% GPT–expert agreement as supporting a practical proxy rather than full expert evaluation. It adds noncausal qualifications for annotation-time associations and speculative explanations involving pretraining and domain-model task mismatch. Conversely, v1's explicit cautions about absent in-person context, demographic imbalance, and broader generalization are not retained in the discussion.

D1.justification: v2 supplements existing implementation details with credential-verification methods and counts, randomized answer ordering, consent and licensing disclosures, and prompts/settings for the added experiments. Core decoding parameters, length limits, hardware, and the code/data link remain. It removes the $20–$35 annotator compensation disclosure and the exact count of six manually replaced questions.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion shifts substantially from counseling dialogues and single-turn versus multi-turn evaluation to medical QA, clinician-grounded evaluation, and adversarial testing. v2 adds positioning against MedQA, MedMCQA, HealthBench, MHQA, and mental-health red-teaming studies, while removing much of the discussion and citations concerning counseling-dialogue datasets and therapist biases.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and concluding discussion are extensively rewritten. Research questions become a contribution list, related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, and terminology shifts toward mental-health QA. New annotation-analysis, ethics, and reproducibility sections accompany substantial reorganization of the appendices.

P2.justification: v2 removes the expert-rating radar plot, redraws the judge comparison with nine models and revised colors/legends, and expands the adversarial table into zero-shot and few-shot panels. It adds several analytical tables and moves the sentence-detection comparison into the appendix. Typography, headings, table pagination, and figure placement also change substantially.

improvement.justification: Added annotation documentation, mitigation tests, specialized-model diagnostics, and more measured claims make v2 easier to assess. These gains are limited by removal of explicit limitations and new inconsistencies: Appendix C's 460-pair accounting is unclear, and the claimed GPT-5 ranking exception is unsupported by Tables 1 and 14. The added evidence and transparency provide a modest net benefit rather than a substantial overall improvement.
